newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-NZ Refining sees depressed margins.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-NZ Refining sees depressed margins.

text.p: New Zealand Refining Co Ltd General Manager Graham Searle said on Friday that downward pressure on oil refining margins, relative to historical levels, was likely to remain over the next two years before an upturn was likely.
"Over the next two years our view is that margins will remain weak, relative to historical levels," Searle said in an interview.
"We would certainly not expect margins to be above US$4.00 a barrel and probably closer to $3.00 for our situation," Searle said. "After that I think they will improve."
Searle said there had been a significant structural shift in the South East Asian region as increased capacity came on stream. Margins generally had become more volatile.

"Up until last year, the Far East region, including Australasia, has really always been a net importer of product," he said. Much of the new capacity had come on stream in the first half of this year.

Searle said it was significant that for the first time the regional industry had seen a major product go into surplus -- gasoline. "The additional capacity has caused the region to go long gasoline and it appears to be structurally long," he said.
But margins for middle distillate -- gas oil and jet fuel -- were still strong and increased capacity had done nothing other than keep pace with demand.
"The refineries that are predominantly configured to produce middle distillate have been looking at much better margins -- maybe US$3.50-$4.00 a barrel," he said.
Just over half of NZ Refining's production is in middle distillate and under 30 percent is in gasoline.
Refining margins are calculated in U.S. dollars, leaving NZ Refining open to the rise in the New Zealand dollar.
"If we look at 1996, margins have been better than the company had expected, but just slightly better."
But Searle said NZ Refining had countered the six percent rise in the New Zealand dollar in 1995 by cutting costs by seven percent. He also expected cost cuts of 5-6 percent in the current year.
Searle said NZ Refining's recent expansion would allow the company to increase middle distillate capacity by about 10 percent.
The company's third quarter was better than anticipated.
"The third quarter was as good in terms of income returns as the first half of the year was, so in that respect we have not seen a particular slowdown," he said.
But Searle said the second half would not be as profitable as the first, when the company made a net profit of NZ$27.61 million.
He said NZ Refining was not relying on margins to improve overnight, but he believed there were opportunities to increase throughput.
There was also potential for growth in line with growth in domestic demand for oil products in New Zealand.

The board had recently approved an investment of just under NZ$10 million to increase the "run length" of its hydrocracker to two years from the present 12 to 16 months and reducing maintenance downtime.
"That's actually worth a huge amount to us as every day the unit is down it costs us between NZ$300,000-$500,000 in lost income," Searle said.
